I finished this in 2 days, and while I love the visuals and the geometric portraits, I didn't find this story compelling enough to have really enjoyed it. There were no obvious typos or grammar issues but at times the dialogue didn't feel natural, I suppose in part that comes down to the restriction of having to express rage or disbelief in a text message. 

There were enough threads to keep busy, not so many that it'd be frustrating trawling through evidence, but since the relevant page is highlighted for you, it's not very challenging, and I could see certain twists coming. I would also have like more to the game mechanics rather than solely dragging and dropping data chunks. 

Basically, it's an interactive story founded on a great idea, but didn't meet its potential for me.

So, I just finished my first play through of Orwell, and I'm not quite sure how I feel about this game. First off, if you don't like reading, don't get this. I feel like it's pretty obvious, but everything is text based, not even voice acting. Which, is fine, I just want whoever may read this to know what they are getting themselves into. I spent about 3 hours on this, and I won't say I had a great time and excited to give it another shot, but I definitely don't regret the time I've put into this either. Second, is there replayability to this? My gut instinct is to say yes. However, with no feeling of excitement to start this all over, I am not entirely sure. If I do replay it, are there different endings? I get the impression there is, but that brings me back to not having much of a desire to replay it. The term "hacker" got thrown around A LOT. It was a bit cheesy, but it didn't really break the entertainment. Also, the amount of twists happening. I get that it's a sort of mystery game, but oh my lord did that get tiresome. There is a twist at the very end (or at least the ending I got, if there are multiple endings) and I just thought it was a bit forced. I wasn't in shock, I kinda just sighed and thought to myself "let's just get this over with".

My ultimate verdict is, get this game if it's on sale. It wasn't a waste of 3 hours of my life, because there were a few times where I was excited to see what would happen next, but after finishing it, I'm sitting here just feeling ehh. It was entertaining, but I'm glad I bought it on sale.

This game feels like a visual novel. You are in charge of gathering information on different suspects of a terrorist attack with the help of Orwell a software that gather information from social media, phone calls, emails...

Pros:
Good story and concept.
Great Design
Shows how easy it is to make a profile of someone from what you can gather on the internet

Cons:
Lack of real choices or intelligent ones. The software preselects whatever information you want to add to the suspects profiles and forces you to choose between "conflicting" information, but an individual thoughts are not black or white. Most people tweet stuff that they regret later or that do not represent there views...
Bugs. The software sends you notification to read new information and add it or not to the profiles, but sometimes it doesn't work. Either doesn't show a notification or notifies you of something you already read or already added to the profile. Which leads, sometimes to reread every piece of information to find the one entry you missed in order to continue to the next chapter.

After a couple of hours I felt it was not very enjoyable to hunt for new information or get blocked on a chapter for a while even though the game tells you that you can omit to upload information to the suspect profiles...
I still think it is a great idea but they should leave more decisions to the player and don't block the player from continuing through the story. If the player didn't find enough evidence than he will not find the culprit --> Game over rather than be stopped from advancing.

[b]Good grief, this game is awful for all the right reasons![/b]
I originally bought this game because of the artstyle and the "UI-based gameplay" rather than another FPS or platformer. I did not expect to get roped into an hour long, complicated, dangerous and honestly mindboggeling conflict between The Nation and it's citizens. But I can't say that I regret it...

Honestly, the game is absolutely amazing. The many characters feel full and alive, with unique personalities and even their own way of typing, which is an incredible level of attention to detail. The game had me so immersed I was actually feeling dread for these characters, and felt so responsible (read: guity) for what happened to them. The story twists and turns many times in a chapter, to the point where it can at times be difficult to follow along, but luckily it always ends up making sense.
The game tackles a very relevant topic in a way that never tells you what to think, but forces you to truly think about it anyways. I found myself halfways through the game suddenly realising that I had started on the side of the citizens, but became more and more interested in preserving myself, and more importantly the Governments interests, which kinda made me [i] super uncomfortable with myself [/i]. But sometimes that's really what you need with topics like these. And getting it with fun gameplay, intense plottwists, characters you quickly bond with and soundtrack and soundcues exactly on point was an experience for sure.
It's not the longest game, but also not the biggest price so it adds up.

As for the ending tho, and this is where the game visibly lacks...
[spoiler] The ending kinda hit me out of left field, and all the loose ends kinda just unraveled even more. Uncovering the fact that Abraham was dead was a shocker for sure, but it got messy when trying to figure out when he immigrated, why the obituary was in his old name, when he died. I barely got time to figure it all out before the ending came crashing. Juliet being the bomber felt... Very out of the blue. Maybe I just missed something sure, but there didn't seem to be a lot of clues that she was the type of person to do such a thing, and she still doesn't. The limit on data-uploads really added stress to the game, but also made it feel very tight, and so made the rest of the ending feel haphazard and like it was just trying to get out of the way as quick as possible...[/spoiler]

All in all: [i] god this game is good[/i]
Absolutely reccomended if you want to yell "Wait what?!" out loud at your screen multiple times. Or if you're really craving a headache with a side of Relevant Politics.

Orwell is an information game, meaning you, bit by bit, uncover the story by puzzling together information pieces.

Sometimes it feels a bit too on the nose though and occasionally I found information that should have been important but was not interactable.

Additionally it is a bit buggy and kind of unstable.
The most annoying bug for me was the missing tooltip on hovering over an information piece and I experienced one crash to desktop.

All in all I had a good time with it and will now play the sequel.

In my very first playthrough, I reported a suspect as armed and dangerous, and lethal force was subsequently authorized. I'd just spent the past half-hour getting to know this person; I was slightly sympathetic to their situation, and I felt physically ill after realizing I might've rubber-stamped their execution without a second thought.
"Just following orders" indeed.

Here's my takeaway:
[h1]Orwell is a nuanced, moving, and above all [b]topical[/b] exploration of the maxim "Information is Power" and its ramifications in the Digital Age.[/h1]

This game really impressed me. I love how the story starts out simple and you tell yourself "This should be easy, just find proof x is this type of person". Then it progresses to making excuses and trying to justify why you had to make a certain decision, once you see the consequences of your actions. 

This game requires a lot of reading and detective work but don't let that fool you. It is very fast paced. Something that looks like a simple detail might be what can uncover a whole lot. This makes it difficult for you to decide which information is relevant. 

I recommend the game for people who love investigative and narrative driven games. Your choices are important so choose wisely :)

A unique take on Orwellian philosophical ideals presented through interactive means, with the Player through gameplay mechanics being forced to utilize a totalitarian and invasive computer program. While having a clear political stance regarding the advantages/disadvantages of such program, the game through amazing writing (and no voice-acting!) creates some of the most memorable characters and dilemmas in recent years. With a humane yet intelligent insight on why thought and freedom of thinking are abandoned concepts in our modern social media era, Orwell creates intense emotional moments through mere text messages and news articles. By simple choices made by the Player, the success and failures of both the program and the revolutionary ideals are affected, and through interactivity the dilemmas of privacy invasion takes its own unique turn. Definitely a game for anyone wanting both a harrowing story and an artistic experience that can't be told in another medium.

Right off the bat, anyone who actually made it through their reading list in highshool English class would most likely predict any new game titled ‘Orwell’ might be about to try and thematically explore both technological authoritarianism and very grey morality. In this case, you’d be right, and this new Orwell sees to ape the mechanisms of power in its namesake’s classic ‘Nineteen Eighty-Four’, but now with a slick Twenty-First Century look, a whole new lexicon of doubleplusgood compound word gibberish, and by placing you – the player – behind the controls of the surveillance state’s nightmare machine. 

The premise of Orwell is that you are the most recent new recruit at the security department of a ruthless, modern, one-party dictatorship’s unfeeling government office and are being assigned to the task of monitoring a national database’s worth of information through little more than mouse control click-and-scroll from your work-issue laptop. The slightly dubious nature of having an inexperienced new hire involved in top-level security quickly proves useful when your “impartiality” sees you assigned to the task of using your new toolset to find the culprit(s) behind a recent bombing at a public park political demonstration.            

The gameplay itself is initially interesting, and certainly unique among what games I’ve seen, however, when you’re several hours in and starting to wind up the story, it might start to feel a bit samey and unchallenging. Essentially the central puzzle at hand at any given time is navigating one of your open browser pages to read or listen to the right excerpt of information, then follow a hyperlink on that page until the story eventually runs through all its possible strands and you get some new pile of expy social media pages to comb through. I can’t say I found the story itself to be anything hugely impressive, and despite the game’s store page and other Reviews implying an ability to sway a branching plot, that isn’t really the case in any major sense.

I’ll go ahead and officially Recommend Orwell on the basis of its high level of polish, full Steam community integration (Trading Cards, Achievements, Chat Emotes, and all the rest) and an extensive effort by the devs to continue patching in further international language support. But apart from that, I can’t strictly say you should pick this game up unless it’s on sale, and/or, or just really want to try this specific sort of art-project-come-‘game’.

Modern-day 1984 (as if the name wasn't hint enough). Search people's emails, texts, phone calls for evidence. Search newspapers, blogs, and so on for evidence. Use this evidence to slowly uncover what the government has been up to as well spying on some citizens to see how they're connected and if they're involved in some recent terrorist attacks.

Don't go into this expecting this to be a mystery where you use your brain to solve crimes by spying on people. It's not. It's more like a visual novel, and like a visual novel there's a lot of railroading. All the data you need (and some you don't; you get to decide which to upload, though some data is needed to progress the story) is highlighted for you in the documents you read. Not only that, but the documents where said data is are marked so you can find them easily. 

That being said, I found this game surprisingly enjoyable! I actually felt bad spying on people, and I'll admit there were several "oops" moments where I felt even worse, not realizing what the consequences of revealing certain information would be until after the fact. The story had me engaged, I liked the characters who all had their own unique voices and stories to tell as you spied on their lives. 

Only minor quibble I can think of is the writing: this needed a few more rounds of editing. Grammatical mistakes, spelling errors, and punctuation errors were frequent enough to be noticed, but not enough to detract or distract from the story. A lot of the writing was unpolished, which is fine in text messages between friends, but not when you're reading a supposedly top-of-the-line news article from the government.

Some of the reveals in conversations felt a bit forced for the sake of moving the story along, too, but again, extreme nitpicking. This is a great game and I'd recommend it to everyone and anyone.

In this investigation game , your job is to examine facts and determine which ones are relevant and should be fed into the system. Your choices affect the decisions that Orwell and law enforcement make, and most of all, the people you are investigating. Government surveillance is a slippery slope.

Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You is a short game where you are given the ability to investigate people's online interaction where a group of people orchestrates bomb attacks taken place in a seemingly dialogue interactive game. You are given the ability to explore the internet, browse through files, remotely access suspect's PC and also tap into their phone calls/messages to find out and expose the truth. 

Pros:
+ Loved the artwork of the game
+ Processing data chunks gives you great detail on what's important and what's going on, and sometimes you'll have to deal with conflicting data
+ Engaging story with plot twists
+ Spying on people during their messages/phone calls felt realistic and almost makes you feel like you're dealing with a real person
+ Gave me some laughs when I was nitpicking with irrelevant data chunks
+ Story has different directions
+ The tense music felt great
+ Dialogues and texts were very well-written

Cons:
- Very short game

Only get it on sale though. Game hour/dollar ratio is bad.

TLDR: This is a very different and morally challenging game. The game play itself is easy but the story is really in depth and there are many choices that have severe consequences. It is short, but it has great replayability to explore how different choices affect the world. Definitely pick it up!

Orwell has a compelling story set in a dystopian maybe-not-so-future where the government has begun a program to monitor any and everything in real time.

The story was very good, however, to experience all of the options you have to replay the full game. There are several 7+ minute conversations paced out painfully slowly. I get that the pacing is set to make it feel like you're monitoring this real time (and that's important in a few cases!) but the majority of the time, pretty much any time there isn't tense music going on, the game needs an option to skip through the snoozefest that is the communications system. I legitimately got up, made myself a meal, and came back to find one segment still running. What was an engaging and interesting storyline the first time around became a complete drag by the end.

If you're not a lore-focused gamer, you'll hate this game. If you're a fast reader, you'll hate this game. If you're a slow reader who likes good stories, this is the game for you.

I got this game on sale, and I'm glad I did because it's only really good for one play through. I was strongly compelled by the storyline, but my decisions in-game didn't heavily factor in to vast majority of the narrative, which made it more of a novel. Pros: The art is great, the sound atmosphere is good, the story is strong, and the dialogue around security vs. privacy is handled masterfully, but, Cons: it only takes a few hours to get through and the majority of the storyline is set in stone before the player weighs in. Something I would have liked to see the game creators lean into more is the security footage access, which is only featured at the very beginning of the game. The fact that it's left out for the remainder seems like a plot hole in a story where Orwell is tapped in to everything. I strongly agree with other players that the highlighting of relevant information babies the player through the document-sifting, and would have liked more of a challenge there. But, they did a good job world building with those documents, you just have to have the patience to ignore the highlights and read all of them to get a full grasp of the characters and their society. It was such a compelling narrative I only left the computer once while playing, and I'll definitely be playing the sequel.

Orwell reminds me of the old "Choose Your Own Adventure" books I enjoyed in my youth.  The story gives the player a real sense of agency in the outcome of the plot.  I found myself developing personal opinions about the characters and becoming interested in details about their lives that were most likely irrelevant to my investigation.  I've only played the story once, but I do want to play again and explore other possibilities.  

That being said, I do think the game has a couple weaknesses.  It can feel like "work" (but you are playing from the vantage point of a person working remotely on an investigation).  I wish there were a few more cutscenes like the opening sequence to create variety.  Additionally, I found myself grinding through certain parts of the game where I couldn't find the relevant data needed to progress the story.  Lastly, the ending struck me as abrupt.  I made a choice about a piece of data, and that was the end.

The game that lets you be the judge, jury, and perhaps executioner.  How do you feel about big brother?

Orwell is an excellent puzzle/detective-type game which has you working for a national surveillance test, poring over news articles, social media, phone calls, emails, text messages, you know it!

The setup is very straightforward, who is the terrorist responsible?  Finding out will require a lot of reading of materials, sometimes many times, as you select "data chunks" to give to the Orwell program for analysis (and potentially new materials to look over!)  In that way the play is quite simple, just drag and drop highlighted data, but be careful!  Not all data is current, and some data conflicts!  You also need to take into account the personalities of the people you are investigating, are they hiding something? Are they boastful?  Be aware that in many ways, you will reap what you sow.

The game is pretty simple to play, in my opinion, and you are basically being hand-held over the first in-game day.  The challenge comes from the narrative you want to put into Orwell, will you seek out the truth or serve the state?  Something that was very unexpected for me was the emotional response to events in the game.  At one point I actually cried: I prevented a catastrophe, saving lives, which felt very good, but it laid bare the potential effectiveness of a system that seeks to remove all privacy and could have went wrong very easily.

I also want to say something to the more pessimistic or paranoid about games where you serve something 'evil' and close to reality: this is a story-puzzle game, and has a very defined message.  A CIA AI tutor it is not.

I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a good mystery and most especially likes to read.  I wish there were more games where you teeter on the edge of being a web junkie and a librarian, ha!

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a truly immerse adventure experience. The mechanics are intuitive and organic, as such, there is a bit of a learning curve in the beginning. The game still has new tricks to teach you even in later stages, as you realize exactly how much you can do, and how it mimics real life. The "interface" for the game is itself a computer screen. You shift through various types and sources of information, trying to differentiate what is real from what isn't, and resolving inherent contradictions. Any mistakes you make could impact the course of the game and the outcomes of the "case" you are working and the characters, who are complex, "real" feeling characters whose fates you can easily begin to care about as the plot progresses. The story is engrossing, and excellently written, with lots of potential twists and turns. The gameplay gets very meta near the end, and the choices you make matter - as have the ones who have made throughout the earlier game. I got the sense that there were many different variables that could result in many different outcomes at the end. 

I played through the game in almost 5 hours and I'm excited to do another run through in the future. It's definately something you want to experience in a single sitting for best results, and the length and depth of the game is perfect for this. I normally am not eager to replay a game, but with this one I can't hardly wait.

It's really hard for me to determine whether I do or don't recommend this, as I'm right on the line. I think overall, though, I have to lean into not recommending it.

The game starts off really well, with a really balanced juxtaposition of people being concerned about privacy versus the very real result of what you're able to accomplish through spying, really highlighting the blurred line between privacy and security. Further, the fact that there are rules in place - such as you can't hack someone without what is essentially a warrant from higher up in the system - makes it feel more grounded, and honestly like a more fair system. 

However, as you reach the end of the game, this completely falls apart. In the closing act, you get beaten around the head with the game designers' opinion, which is a very black-and-white "spying bad, privacy good", which entirely undermines the nuance the entire game up until that point had executed so well. I'll save the spoiler-filled rant for the end.

In addition to this, the gameplay has some glaring flaws. There are certain pieces of information that you absolutely [i]must[/i] collect to move forward, which is sometimes information that seems completely irrelevant (and you're outright told not to submit irrelevant information), forcing you to comb through every possible source with a fine-toothed comb, and sometimes just guess what they want you to submit.

Also, you can only extract verbatim phrases to submit, devoid of any context or clarification. Often, this leads to bizarre interpretations from the game. Like, apparently the game makers think [spoiler]that Depression or PTSD are things that make someone dangerous, rather than being a potentially debilitating disability[/spoiler]. Or perhaps you want to flag one piece of information because of it's context, but because that context isn't part of the auto-selected snippet, the game completely misinterprets it. For example, [spoiler]one girl is in a relationship with a guy, and helps herself to his wallet to make a couple purchases. Any reasonable person would have enough context to say, "Oh, she's borrowing his wallet, and he's only mildly annoyed that she's spending a lot? Clearly they are in a very serious relationship." How about the game? "She took his wallet? She has a history of theft! She's clearly a criminal!"[/spoiler] Like, wtf?

So that's why I just can't recommend this game. Despite the promise it shows, it really undermines itself, especially in the final stretch.

Now, about that endgame rant... Endgame spoilers follow: [spoiler]You reach the end of the game, and basically get lectured at by someone who (1) organized multiple bombings that killed dozens of people, (2) lied to and manipulated multiple friends to do her dirty work, ruining their lives, and (3) is completely unrepentant (going with the "can't make an omelet without breaking a few eggs" excuse). What's worse, is that she did all this to protest the whole mass-spying thing, but the only reason you're even spying on anyone in that community is because of the bombings! Literally, she created the problem that she's complaining about.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]Meanwhile, you (potentially) used [i]your[/i] minor sin of spying to save dozens or even hundreds of lives at the mall [i]she[/i] tried to bomb - targeting civilians to make people care more about her message. She also blames you for sending police in who end up killing her friend, just because, you know, they actually [i]were[/i] guilty of setting bombs to kill people, and opened fire on the police. How dare those cops return fire on a known bomber who is armed and dangerous just because she shot first![/spoiler]

[spoiler]And what's worse, is that all the other people involved in the plot-device-conference-call at the end [i]take her side![/i] Like, [i]really?[/i] In the end, you're basically pushed to take down the entire system you've been a part of, despite the fact that the game shows it doing an objectively good job of keeping people safe and bringing conspiracies to justice, because spying is bad, just, end of story, just take our word for that.[/spoiler]
Also makes for a cautionary tale of where your information is right now.
